verdicts.why: The brief explicitly states the choir owns hundreds of scores stored in a cupboard.
The rough idea explicitly mentions a forty-person choir.

The brief does not state there is no catalog; it says nobody knows what they have, but the librarian maintains a catalog per the workflow answer — the pain point is that she is the sole human search engine, not that no catalog exists.
The brief directly states the goal is so 'the librarian stops being a human search engine,' matching this statement precisely.
The success criterion of 'every borrowed copy traceable to a member' implies current tracking is absent or inadequate.
The rough idea and success criteria confirm the project will build a catalog with borrowing tracking.
The scripted answers explicitly state the librarian maintains the catalog, so the administrator is known — not unknown.
The scripted answers explicitly list the required fields (title, composer, arrangement, copy count), so this is not unknown.
No scripted answer addresses overdue reminders or escalation, so this is a genuine unknown not covered by the brief.
The stated success signal is no duplicate purchases and traceable borrows, not reducing librarian interruptions; the self-service implication is an added inference not supported by the brief.

The brief explicitly states 'no sheet music scans in scope,' indicating a decision was made but framing it as deferred is close enough — however the brief does say it is out of scope, making this partially misleading; still, the topic of digital scores is addressed and marked out of scope, which is grounded.
The scripted answers explicitly state roughly 400 titles.
The range of 10–50 copies per title and 400 titles are stated facts; the arithmetic derivation (4,000–20,000) follows directly.
The scripted answers explicitly list title, composer, arrangement, and copy count as the fields that matter.
The scripted answers explicitly state 'no sheet music scans in scope,' confirming digital scanning is out of scope.

payload.why: Data migration effort is a reasonable operational concern, but the brief's most critical unknowns are scope (number of titles/copies, data fields) and the distinct user roles—both of which directly shape minimum-viable features. Those questions would unlock more architectural value at turn 1 than asking about onboarding logistics.

The spec is sufficient on catalog and borrowing basics but is notably padded with multiple speculative gaps flagged as open concerns (technical comfort, hosting, cost, data retention, backup, measurable success thresholds) that were never answered and should not appear as scope-shaping items in a seed artifact. More critically, the spec omits the three distinct user roles (librarian, member, conductor) and the conductor's programme-planning use case that were explicitly scripted, meaning a first vertical slice could miss a confirmed user type entirely — making this both padded with invented uncertainty and missing real asserted scope.
